title: Psalm 88: Darkness Is My Closest Companion
summary: A man who has suffered since his youth cries to God day and night from the edge of death. He feels God's wrath sweeping over him like waves, his friends have turned from him, and he asks whether the dead can praise God. The psalm never turns to confidence or thanks; it ends with the words that darkness is his closest companion.

from.where: The Study Bible's notes on Psalm 88

line: A man who has suffered since his youth cries to God day and night from the edge of death, his friends gone; the psalm never turns to trust, and it ends in darkness.
guide: Psalm 88 does not ask you to feel anything; it gives words to someone already in the dark, or sitting beside someone who is. Let it stand as it is, without rushing to a happier ending, and pray it as your own; the prayer still counts. If you are not in the dark, pray it for someone who is.

care.text: Psalm 88 does not end with hope, and these notes will not give it a happier ending than the Bible gives it. If you are reading this psalm because it sounds like your life, it is not a sign that your faith has failed. The man who prayed it was still praying. That counts.

These notes do not give anyone's suffering a name or a diagnosis. But if darkness feels like your closest companion, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust today: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. Sorrow that lasts, or that takes away sleep, hope or the wish to go on, is worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a lack of faith.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
If someone you love prays like this, stay near them. Listen without hurrying them to the end of the psalm. And help them reach the people who can help.

ending.text: That is where the psalm ends. There is no turn to trust. There is no ‘But I will praise You’. The last word in Hebrew is ‘darkness’.

Most laments in the Psalms move from complaint toward trust. Psalm 13 does. Psalm 6 does. The book page calls Psalm 88 the one lament that never turns. It ends in the dark, and God kept it in the book anyway.

stanzas.title: A cry to the God of salvation
Counted among the dead, overwhelmed by God's wrath
Why do you hide your face? Darkness remains

verses.t: A song. A Psalm of the sons of Korah. For the choirmaster. According to Mahalath Leannoth. A Maskil of Heman the Ezrahite. O LORD, the God of my salvation, day and night I cry out before You.
May my prayer come before You; incline Your ear to my cry.
For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol.
I am counted among those descending to the Pit. I am like a man without strength.
I am forsaken among the dead, like the slain who lie in the grave, whom You remember no more, who are cut off from Your care.
You have laid me in the lowest Pit, in the darkest of the depths.
Your wrath weighs heavily upon me; all Your waves have submerged me. Selah
You have removed my friends from me; You have made me repulsive to them; I am confined and cannot escape.
My eyes grow dim with grief. I call to You daily, O LORD; I spread out my hands to You.
Do You work wonders for the dead? Do departed spirits rise up to praise You? Selah
Can Your loving devotion be proclaimed in the grave, Your faithfulness in Abaddon?
Will Your wonders be known in the darkness, or Your righteousness in the land of oblivion?
But to You, O LORD, I cry for help; in the morning my prayer comes before You.
Why, O LORD, do You reject me? Why do You hide Your face from me?
From my youth I was afflicted and near death. I have borne Your terrors; I am in despair.
Your wrath has swept over me; Your terrors have destroyed me.
All day long they engulf me like water; they enclose me on every side.
You have removed my beloved and my friend; darkness is my closest companion.
